mitigation_mechanism: In this evidence restored forest cover lowers flood peaks moderately, and mainly at local scale and for smaller storms. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; the review attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that the beneficial effects of reforesting, terracing and contouring degraded lands on stormflow and peakflow are evident at small-basin scale, as is the regenerative capacity of most ecosystems when left alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. In a clear-cut Oregon basin, peak discharges recovered gradually as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis expects flash flooding to be reduced locally for frequent short, low-intensity storm events where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a global review states that afforestation in energy-limited environments will help to reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding].
caveats: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. No unit measures a benefit at severe or extreme flood; the only reading at the 1% AEP event is that review's pooled modelled points [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments and the Himalayan essays on forest loss, sit in the protection family row and do not set this class. For farmers the effect is off-site: any reduction arrives downstream of the restored land, not on their plots.

justification.mechanism: In this evidence restored forest cover lowers flood peaks moderately, and mainly at local scale and for smaller storms. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; the review attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that the beneficial effects of reforesting, terracing and contouring degraded lands on stormflow and peakflow are evident at small-basin scale, as is the regenerative capacity of most ecosystems when left alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. In a clear-cut Oregon basin, peak discharges recovered gradually as the basin revegetated, which the authors attribute to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis expects flash flooding to be reduced locally for frequent short, low-intensity storm events where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a global review states that afforestation in energy-limited environments will help to reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding].
justification.conditionality: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. No unit measures a benefit at severe or extreme flood; the only reading at the 1% AEP event is that review's pooled modelled points [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments and the Himalayan essays on forest loss, sit in the protection family row and do not set this class. For farmers the effect is off-site: any reduction arrives downstream of the restored land, not on their plots.

mitigation_mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps; nearly all of it is evidence about existing forest, read through what happens when it is cut. A later analysis of the same basins found large events increased by 25% at Andrews 1, 16% at Andrews 6 and 26% at Coyote 3 after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. Two reviews of forest hydrology state the general rule: after forest cutting or conversion there is usually, in response to each storm, an increase in peak flow, storm-flow volume and storm-flow duration [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_5], and a certain increase in stormflow volume and peakflow cannot be avoided after forest conversion, with the relative increase largest for small events (which may be doubled) and smallest for large ones (perhaps in the order of 10 per cent or less) [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_5]. An FAO synthesis states that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season, and that for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]. justification.mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps; nearly all of it is evidence about existing forest, read through what happens when it is cut. In paired experimental basins in Oregon, a high-income setting, discharges in small basins increased by 50% in the first 5 years after clear-cutting and were 25 to 40% higher than pretreatment up to 25 years later, and forest harvesting with roads has increased peak discharges by as much as 50% in small basins and 100% in large basins over the past 50 years [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_2, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_3, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. A later analysis of the same basins found large events increased by 25% at Andrews 1, 16% at Andrews 6 and 26% at Coyote 3 after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. Two reviews of forest hydrology state the general rule: after forest cutting or conversion there is usually, in response to each storm, an increase in peak flow, storm-flow volume and storm-flow duration [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_5], and a certain increase in stormflow volume and peakflow cannot be avoided after forest conversion, with the relative increase largest for small events (which may be doubled) and smallest for large ones (perhaps in the order of 10 per cent or less) [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_5]. An FAO synthesis states that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season, and that for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]. At the local scale forests and forest soils reduce runoff through enhanced infiltration and storage, and peak flows rise after forest removal in small experimental catchments [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_2]. A country-level analysis of developing countries predicted that a further hypothetical 10% loss of natural forest cover would raise flood frequency by 3.5% to 28.1% and flood duration by 3.8% to 7.9% [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_1, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_2]; in Peninsular Malaysia, a river-basin panel study by Tan-Soo and colleagues found that converting 1% of a basin from inland forest to oil palm increased the number of days flooded by 26.8%, and to rubber by 26.5%, with conversion to urban use also having a large effect (semi-elasticity = 35.9%) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]; a systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds that deforestation consistently increases peak flows [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]; and in Swiss valleys with more than 30% forest, snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk lower [ev_flood_hazard_iufro18_2].
justification.conditionality: Tree-crop farming systems enter this row only through the Malaysian study, where oil palm and rubber are the land uses that replaced inland forest; nothing here measures flood protection for tree-crop farmers themselves [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2]. The harvest studies, the forest-loss analyses and the two classic reviews describe what existing forest does; they enter through the existing-forest comparator (the flood-cover review's deforestation reading among them [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]), which routes them to this protection family and keeps them out of the restoration families, so none of them is a restoration or protection-programme result. The Malaysian study also carries the harm finding in this row: where the forest converted was wetland (peat-swamp) forest, deforestation reduced flooding, a large effect (semi-elasticity = 38.0%), which the authors link to drainage installed at conversion lowering the water level; so keeping forest is not a flood defence in every forest type [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_3]. The same study found no significant effect of deforestation on the number of floods per month, which the authors put down to a problem in defining that variable rather than to forest having no effect [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_5]. Its inland-forest figures are semi-elasticities per 1% of basin area converted, not whole-catchment contrasts, and the oil palm and rubber results are from a single period of conversion, not restoration [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2], while the urban figure was not estimated very precisely (P = 0.094) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]. The Oregon large-basin increase is bundled with forest road construction and is stated as an upper bound, as much as [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. The service fades with storm size and basin size. Complete clear-cutting without roads produced significant increases in fall and winter events but not for large events as a group [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_4], and at Andrews 10 large events did not change after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_2]. In the same study other types of winter events did not change, so only rain-on-snow peaks rose in winter [ev_water_regulation_jon00_7], and in the fog-prone basins changes in cloud water interception apparently offset changes in evapotranspiration in two partially cut basins [ev_water_regulation_jon00_5]. The fall increases came in small events (0.22- or 0.28-year return periods), not in large events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. For the rarer prolonged or high-intensity storms, once the soil layer becomes saturated water will run off even where there is full, undisturbed forest cover [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_4]; Hamilton's earlier essay makes the same point, that for major storms the effect of forest on or forest off is dwarfed by the rainfall itself, since soil can only store so much water [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_6]. He judges that the June 1985 floods that killed 237 persons in six Indian states were caused by too much rain in too short a time, with some areas receiving 414 mm in 24 hours on already saturated soils, and that even a fully forested basin would have flooded; this is his judgement, not data [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_12]. Forest soils reduce runoff only in small-scale rainfall events, which are not responsible for severe downstream flooding, and forests cannot stop catastrophic large-scale floods caused by severe meteorological events [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_2]; and small to medium peak flows are affected most while the largest events do not change noticeably [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_3]. At basin scale the link is not shown. A worldwide review of watershed research found no cause and effect between forest cutting in the headwaters and floods in the lower basin; Hamilton cites it both in his earlier essay, where he adds that there are no valid reasons to suggest forests can prevent major floods on the large rivers of the subcontinent, and in his later FAO synthesis, so this is a single finding [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_4, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_2]. Long records from meso-scale basins of up to 14500 km2 in Taiwan and northern Thailand that had lost much forest showed no systematic trend in flood magnitude, climate dominating, although the review notes that much of that forest loss was probably followed by regeneration rather than cropping [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_8]. A Himalayan analysis contends that on the Himalayan scale human influences, so far, are insignificant [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_2]. The cross-country analysis itself found little evidence that further forest loss changed flood deaths or damage [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_3, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_4], and a reanalysis found the correlation between forest cover or cover loss and flood frequency appears absent [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_1]. Read the slight class as a local, small-to-medium storm service, not a defence against severe or extreme floods. For farmers the effect is off-site, arriving downstream of the protected forest.

mitigation_mechanism: Drought kills planted seedlings during establishment: a review attributes rising mortality of recently outplanted seedlings in dry regions to hotter and drier conditions, and links high rates of seedling mortality at restoration sites in western North America to limiting conditions in the energy and hydrologic cycles [ev_establishment_survival_gross26_1, ev_establishment_survival_gross26_3]. Novel drought is credited with complete restoration failure even with outplanting [ev_establishment_survival_svejcar23_2]. In New Zealand, a community restoration planting of native pioneer trees into former dairy pasture lost part of its young cohort to drought: survival after the 2008 drought within the 2007 planting averaged 78% across all species, while the tea-tree species fared best at 97% for mānuka and 98% for kanuka [ev_climate_shock_laughlin18_1].
caveats: In Australia a short dry spell at planting did not significantly affect sapling survival, the soils having been saturated beforehand [ev_drought_hazard_preece23_1], so short dry spells at planting are not necessarily lethal; what separates it from the losses is drought length and the soil moisture going in. The evidence comes from high-income settings with none from low- or middle-income countries, the complete-failure claim is a perspective piece covering plant restoration generally rather than forests, and the review units cite other studies. The only survival figure is the New Zealand planting, and the study does not separate drought deaths from other causes of mortality [ev_climate_shock_laughlin18_1]; the review units describe raised seedling mortality in dry regions and on restoration sites without putting a figure on it [ev_establishment_survival_gross26_1, ev_establishment_survival_gross26_3]. The Spanish dryland reforestation losses are plantation results, reported in their own family rows, and no longer count toward forest restoration.

mitigation_mechanism: Wind damages planted stands once storms pass a threshold, and the damage grows quickly above it. A review of wind damage to planted and managed forests suggests damage starts when canopy-top hourly wind speeds exceed approximately 8.5 m s−1 and gusts outside the forest exceed 25–30 m s−1, with the level of damage increasing almost exponentially as gust speed rises [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_1]. The same review finds that in the same storm a taller, more mature stand is generally more likely to fail than a shorter younger one [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_2], that new gaps or edges from thinning, harvesting, clear-cutting upwind stands or roads leave the remaining trees particularly vulnerable because they are not acclimated to the new wind conditions [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_3], and that the effects last for many years through further wind or insect damage to weakened trees or reduced growth [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_4]. In central Vietnam typhoon damage is a continuing concern for smallholder plantations and leads planters to favour short-cycle rotations [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_ieg18_1]; on a Spanish dryland reforestation project, windstorms blew away tree shelters [ev_climate_shock_delcampo21_1].
caveats: The class is slight because the field evidence describes manageable losses: the Vietnam evaluation adds that typhoon risk has so far not discouraged smallholders from continuing to plant, the Spanish losses were partly attributed to poor tethering, and the Uganda afforestation compiler judges the technology to cope well with local windstorms [ev_asset_wind_cyclone_ieg18_1, ev_climate_shock_delcampo21_1, ev_asset_wind_cyclone_wocat_1577_2013_local_windstorm]. The review's thresholds come from planted and managed forests mostly in Europe, Japan and New Zealand and cite other studies; it notes that no definitive global values can be given because site and forest conditions differ and trees in windier climates are generally more stable [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_1]. Its findings make management a lever on this threat: rotation length, thinning regime and where edges are created all change the risk [ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_2, ev_climate_shock_gardiner21_3]. Whether the plantation family belongs in the forest-restoration roll-up at all is an open decision for the team, so read this row as plantation evidence, not as restoration toward a natural baseline.
